idiom_name: let constants + value types (struct) with copy-on-write stdlib collections
implementation_notes: Swift's value semantics make the guarantee structural: structs and enums are copied on assignment, and the standard library collections (Array, Dictionary, Set, String) are structs backed by a reference-counted buffer that is copied only when a second reference mutates it, so let bindings are immutable and copies stay cheap until written - that replaces the immutable wrapper class. A struct with let stored properties cannot be mutated through any reference, and because it is a value type no other holder can alias-mutate it; updates are expressed as functions returning a new value. The classic reference-type structure is still justified when identity is required (a class with a lifecycle) or for a large custom buffer that needs its own copy-on-write implementation with isKnownUniquelyReferenced; Objective-C collections keep reference semantics and must be copied.
pitfalls: Value types are shallow: a let struct whose stored property is a class instance shares that mutable object with every copy.

Copy-on-write is per buffer and lazy: writing one element of a shared Array triggers a full copy, so element-wise mutation in a loop can become O(n) per write when the array is not uniquely referenced.
Bridging to Objective-C collections reintroduces reference semantics: NSMutableArray and NSMutableDictionary are shared and mutable, and a Swift copy may share storage until written.
let on a struct prevents mutation through that binding, but a var property of a referenced class can still change.
